aspectTitle: Pointer-only (mouse/touch/gesture) handlers on non-native elements with no keyboard equivalent (F54)
aspectDescription: A function is wired up exclusively through pointing-device events (onclick/onmousedown/onmouseup/onmouseover, or touch/pointer/gesture listeners) on an element that has no native keyboard behaviour and no tabindex, role, or key handler — typically a div, span, img, li, or svg. The page looks fully operable, but a keyboard-only user can never reach or invoke the function. The human-judgment core is recognizing that a given visual control (a 'Next' arrow image, a star-rating widget, a custom 'Add to cart' tile, a swipeable carousel) actually IS interactive functionality whose only trigger is a p
scenario: Restaurant 'Write a review' form whose 5-star overall-rating control is five ★ glyphs, each with inline onclick that sets the rating. No tabindex, no role, no key handler. The name field, review textarea, and native submit button are all keyboard operable, so the only keyboard-dead affordance is the star widget.
mechanism: The rating-setting function is invokable solely through a pointer click on a generic <span>. The spans are not in the tab order and not exposed as controls (no role/tabindex/keydown), so a keyboard-only or switch user can never reach or operate them; there is no alternative keyboard path to set the rating anywhere on the page. Canonical F54: pointing-device-only handler is the sole mechanism to invoke a non-path-dependent function.

scenario: Homeware store 'New arrivals' grid where each product tile is a <div role="link" aria-label="…view product"> that navigates on click. Navigation is bound at runtime via addEventListener('pointerup', …); the card has no tabindex and no keydown. A real keyboard-operable 'Quick view' <button> sits inside each card as the matched accessible control.

The product-open function therefore has no keyboard route via the card. F54 escalated past the linter by adding a valid role+name so static checks pass.

scenario: Ad-platform 'Create campaign' form whose daily-budget control is a custom slider: a draggable thumb <div> on a track wired only with mousedown/mousemove/touchmove. No role=slider, no tabindex, no aria-value*, no arrow-key handler, and no number field anywhere to type the budget. Every other field (name, objective select, date inputs, Save buttons) is keyboard operable.
mechanism: The thumb and track are plain <div>s exposed as generic content and out of the tab order; the value-setting function is bound exclusively to pointer drag events, with no keydown so arrow/Home/End/PageUp-Down do nothing and no alternative number input exists. A keyboard-only user cannot set the budget at all. The drag sets only the endpoint value (a number from a position), not a path, so it is NOT the path-dependent 2.1.1 exception — it is the F54 failure.

The human-judgment core is recognizing that a given visual control (a 'Next' arrow image, a star-rating widget, a custom 'Add to cart' tile, a swipeable carousel) actually IS interactive functionality whose only trigger is a p
scenario: Credit-union money-transfer confirmation screen whose final 'Confirm & send £420.00' action is a <div role="button" tabindex="0"> with a clear accessible name — focusable and ARIA-correct — but activation is wired ONLY to dblclick/pointerup (a 'double-click to confirm' guard) with no keydown/keyup handler, so Enter and Space do nothing. A real keyboard-operable <button>Cancel</button> sits beside it.
mechanism: The tile is exposed as a focusable button with a valid name, so every static signal looks correct; but the activation logic listens only for dblclick and pointerup (gated to pointerType mouse/touch/pen), so neither Enter nor Space — the platform keys a button role implies — invokes the confirm. The transfer cannot be sent from the keyboard at all (only Cancel is keyboard-reachable, which is not an equivalent). Per the Understanding note a custom button may respond to only one key, but it must respond to some key; here it responds to none. F54 with the element fully ARIA-correct and focusable, so the failure is purely missing keyboard activation.

scenario: Furniture product page where the colour chooser appears twice: a labelled native <select id="colour"> (fully keyboard operable) and a row of pointer-only colour chips <li onclick="pickColour(...)"> with no tabindex/role/keydown. Both call the same pickColour() routine; the chips are a mouse shortcut layered on the real menu and are aria-hidden so AT users are routed to the <select>. Boundary PASS variant that sharpens the aspect.
mechanism: Taken alone each <li onclick> is the F54 shape (pointer-only, no tabindex/role/keydown), but 2.1.1 asks whether the FUNCTION is keyboard operable, not whether every visible control is focusable. The colour-selection function is fully available from the keyboard via the labelled <select> (in tab order, arrow/typeahead operable, calls the same pickColour()), and the chips are aria-hidden so screen-reader users use the menu. Because an equivalent keyboard method for the same action exists, this passes 2.1.1 — demonstrating that a pointer-only handler is not automatically a failure.

aspectTitle: Emulated links/controls that are reachable but not truly activatable by keyboard — wrong element, Enter-only, or no-op handler (F42)
aspectDescription: The subtle slice between a bare pointer-only fake control and a properly built one. Markup that reads as compliant (tabindex present, an onkeypress/onkeydown attribute present, role=button/link) but where keyboard ACTIVATION silently fails: (a) a <div tabindex=0 onclick> with no key handler at all — focusable, so it appears 'in the tab order', but Enter/Space do nothing because a div has no implicit activation; (b) an onkeypress that listens ONLY for Enter (keyCode 13) while onclick does the work, so Space (and any keydown-only AT) gets nothing; (c) a handler that calls preventDefault/returns
scenario: UK council-tax services portal. The primary 'Make a payment' service tile is a <div role=button tabindex=0 onclick> with NO key handler at all, sitting between two genuine <a href> tiles. It receives focus and announces as a button (reads as 'in the tab order') but a div has no implicit activation, so Enter/Space do nothing and there is no alternative keyboard path to card payment.
mechanism: Focusable (tabindex=0) + role=button gives a tab stop announced as a button, but only onclick is wired and no keydown/keypress/keyup handler exists; a div has no implicit activation, so keyboard Enter/Space never executes startPayment(). Reachable but not operable. Verified in headless Chromium: focusable=true, Enter-activates=false, Space-activates=false, mouse-click=true.

scenario: Recipe blog card with a matched pair of visually/structurally identical <span role=link tabindex=0> controls: 'Save to recipe box' has onclick AND onkeypress(Enter) so it is operable (passes per the Understanding note), while 'Print this recipe' is byte-for-byte the same except the onkeypress was deleted in a cleanup commit, so its keyboard activation is silently dead. The page's verdict hinges on actually pressing keys on each control, not on attribute inspection.
mechanism: Two sibling pseudo-links share class/role/tabindex/onclick. Save's onkeypress fires saveRecipe() on Enter (conformant Enter-only). Print has no key handler, so Enter and Space never reach printRecipe(); mouse still works. The page fails because the in-scope Print function is keyboard-reachable but not operable. Verified: Save Enter-activates=true; Print Enter-activates=false and Space-activates=false; both mouse-activate.

scenario: Museum virtual-exhibitions gallery where each clickable cover enters a virtual room. Each has onclick AND an onkeypress, so it appears keyboard-wired, but the handleKey handler calls event.preventDefault() and returns false BEFORE any activation branch — so for every key, including Enter and Space, it stops default behaviour and exits without calling enterRoom(). The key handler is present but swallows activation; no fallback control exists.
mechanism: The element is focusable with a button role and accessible name (alt) and has an onkeypress, so all static keyboard signals are satisfied. But the handler body does event.preventDefault(); return false; making the if(Enter/Space) enterRoom() branch unreachable, so the dialog never opens from the keyboard. Mouse onclick is untouched. Verified: Enter-activates=false, Space-activates=false, mouse-click=true.

scenario: Cloud-console deployments table where each row has a 'more actions' kebab built as <div role=button tabindex=0 aria-haspopup aria-expanded onclick onkeydown>. It looks like a textbook keyboard-ready menu button, but the onkeydown handler gates on event.charCode against 13/32 — and charCode is ALWAYS 0 on a keydown event — so the Enter/Space branch never matches and the menu (containing Redeploy/Roll back/View logs) cannot be opened by keyboard in any browser.
mechanism: kebabKey reads event.charCode on a keydown event; charCode is only ever populated for keypress (and only printing characters), so it is 0 for Enter and Space, 0===13||0===32 is false, toggleMenu() is never called and aria-expanded stays false. The menu items have no other keyboard path. Verified in headless Chromium: Enter-activates=false, Space-activates=false, mouse-click=true (fails universally, not a single-browser quirk; confirmed via Gemini that charCode is 0 on keydown in all current browsers and that window.event would NOT have failed because all browsers now populate it).

scenario: Online-banking transfer form whose primary control is a custom <span role=button tabindex=0 onclick onkeydown(Enter only)> 'Review transfer'. It is focusable and activates on Enter but deliberately does NOT respond to Space. This is the PASS boundary: a naive reviewer who presses Space, sees nothing, and fails it would be wrong — the WCAG Understanding note states a custom control reacting only to Enter still satisfies 2.1.1. The action is both reachable and executable by keyboard and the rest of the form is operable, so the page passes.

aspectTitle: Drag-and-drop / endpoint-style functions without the path exception, lacking a keyboard equivalent (G90 / G202 / Understanding)
aspectDescription: The SC exempts only functions whose input depends on the PATH of movement, not just the endpoints (free-hand drawing, watercolour). Reordering a list by drag, dragging a file into a dropzone, sorting kanban cards, dragging a map pin, or resizing a panel are endpoint-dependent and therefore do NOT qualify for the exception — they REQUIRE a keyboard equivalent (cut/paste, move up/down buttons, an 'enter position' field, type-to-set coordinates). Two human judgments no checker can make: (1) decide whether a given drag operation is genuinely path-dependent (exempt) or merely endpoint-dependent (mu
scenario: Fresh&Co grocery shopping-list reorderable ONLY by native HTML5 drag-and-drop (draggable=true + dragstart/dragover/drop + insertBefore). Every other control (Add form, picked checkboxes) is keyboard-operable, but the reorder function has no keyboard route: no Move-up/Move-down buttons, no position field, and the li items are not focusable and have no key handlers.
mechanism: Reordering a list is endpoint-dependent (only the destination index matters, not the pointer path), so the SC 2.1.1 path-of-movement exception does NOT apply and the function requires a keyboard equivalent. None exists anywhere on the page, so the reorder function is operable by pointer only — a pointing-device-specific mechanism is the sole way to invoke a non-path-dependent function (F54).

scenario: Northwind Talent job-application page. Attaching a resume is required. A native <input type=file id=resume> exists with an associated <label>, but it is display:none and is NEVER surfaced to keyboard users: no clickable/visible <label>, no button calling resume.click(), and the dashed 'Drag your resume file here' area is a plain <div> with only dragover/drop handlers (no role, no tabindex, no key handler). The dropzone div is not focusable/has no key handler, and the display:none input is never reachable (removed from tab order, never .click()-ed), so a keyboard user cannot attach the required resume — pointer-only mechanism (F54). A hidden input with a clickable <label for> or a button calling .click() would pass; the difference is purely keyboard reachability.

scenario: Stripe-style API-reference reader with a draggable splitter between a nav pane and content pane. The splitter is marked up as a textbook ARIA window-splitter — role=separator, aria-orientation=vertical, aria-valuemin/max/now, an aria-label, and tabindex=0 (focusable) — but has NO keydown handler, so arrow keys do nothing and aria-valuenow never changes. scenario: Meridian Bank auto-loan e-signing page. The borrower draws their handwritten signature in a <canvas> with finger/stylus/mouse; strokes are captured free-hand via pointermove and the recorded value is the literal shape of the curves. Every other function (Clear signature button, Type-your-legal-name field, Agree & sign submit) is keyboard-operable. The canvas carries a descriptive accessible name. scenario: Canvasly brand-kit colour editor with a classic HSV picker: a 2D saturation/brightness square (drag the handle anywhere inside) plus a hue slider below. The hue slider is a native <input type=range> — fully focusable and arrow-key operable. aspectTitle: Hover/pointer-only revealed content carrying essential information or controls, with no keyboard path (Trusted Tester essential-information branch)
aspectDescription: Content or controls that appear only on mouseover/hover (CSS :hover dropdowns/megamenus, JS mouseover tooltips, hover-revealed action buttons on table rows or cards) with no focus/keyboard trigger and no equivalent elsewhere. Trusted Tester explicitly splits the SC into operable-functionality AND access-to-essential-information, and gives the precise tooltip nuance: place keyboard focus and if the information does not appear within two seconds, keyboard focus will not reveal it — then ask whether that information is available elsewhere on the page. Two human judgments: (1) is the hover-reveale
scenario: County government site whose primary mega-menu submenus (Pay water bill, Apply for marriage license, Pay traffic ticket, Register to vote) open only on li:hover via CSS, with no :focus-within or JS focus handler; keyboard users can activate the top-level links but the specific essential service deep-links are never tab stops and exist nowhere else on the page.
mechanism: ul.submenu is display:none except under `nav.primary > ul > li:hover ul.submenu`; display:none removes the second-level <a href> service links from the tab order, and there is no :focus-within rule or keydown handler, so keyboard focus never reveals or reaches them — the page's primary government functions are pointer-only.

aspectTitle: Scripts that remove or steal focus the moment it is received (F55) — focus cannot rest on a control
aspectDescription: Content that would normally receive focus has that focus stripped by script (onfocus="this.blur()", a handler that immediately moves focus elsewhere, or a focusin listener that bounces focus back to the top on every Tab). The element appears in the tab order and is technically reachable, but focus cannot remain on it long enough to operate it, so keyboard operation is impossible. This is dynamic behaviour: the static DOM shows a normal, well-formed, focusable control — only by actually tabbing through and watching where focus lands does a human discover focus being yanked away. The judgment is
scenario: Credit-union online-banking sign-in form. The username/password fields are operable, but the primary submit control carries onfocus="this.blur()" (the canonical F55 one-liner). A keyboard user can Tab to the Sign in button but focus is stripped the instant it lands, throwing focus to <body>, so the button can never be activated by keyboard.
mechanism: Inline onfocus HTML event-handler attribute on a native <input type=submit> synchronously calls this.blur() when the element receives focus, so focus is removed on receipt and relocated to document.body; the named, focusable control cannot retain focus to be operated.

scenario: German municipal services portal (de-DE). The site-search field has a mis-wired 'select on focus' helper whose early-return branch calls document.body.focus(). scenario: Newspaper article page with a sticky masthead. A page-wide document focusin listener re-focuses the masthead logo on every focus change ('keep the brand the anchor'), and its exclusion guard compares the wrong property so it never excludes anything. Every Tab to a section-nav link, an article-tool button, the newsletter field, or an in-article link snaps focus back to the logo, freezing the whole page at the masthead for keyboard users.
mechanism: A document-level focusin listener relocates focus to a fixed element (#brandLogo) whenever ANY downstream control receives focus (the guard if(e.tabIndex===logo) is always falsy because FocusEvent has no tabIndex), so every interactive control on the page loses focus on receipt and cannot be operated by keyboard.

scenario: E-commerce storefront newsletter overlay (role=dialog, aria-modal). A marketing-popup plugin's focus management is a modal-scoped focusin listener that re-focuses the email input on every focus-in, with no exclusion for Close (x), the decline link, or Submit. A keyboard user can never Tab off the email field: every attempt to reach Close/Submit rebounds to the email box, so the overlay can neither be dismissed nor submitted by keyboard.
mechanism: A modal-scoped focusin listener defers (setTimeout 0) and re-focuses a single element (the first input) on every focus-in, so the dismiss/submit controls receive focus momentarily then have it stripped and re-granted to the email field. This is a 2.1.1 'focus cannot rest' failure (focus actively relocated to one element), distinct from a 2.1.2 Tab-cycle trap.

scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard with a custom APG 'Date range' listbox (role=button trigger + role=listbox/option, correct aria-expanded/aria-selected, full Arrow/Enter/Escape). It opens by keyboard, but each option has a deferred self-blur added to fix a flicker: on the option's focus event a setTimeout(0) later calls opt.blur() then trigger.focus(). The ring flashes on an option then snaps back to the trigger, so no option can be selected by keyboard.
mechanism: A per-option focus handler asynchronously (setTimeout 0) blurs the option and re-focuses the trigger on every option focus, so options are reachable via Arrow keys but focus is removed on receipt and relocated to the trigger — no option can retain focus to be activated/selected by keyboard.

scenario: Rich-text document-editor toolbar over a contenteditable. Each formatting button declines focus ONLY on pointer interaction via mousedown -> e.preventDefault() (the standard pattern that keeps the caret in the editor when you click Bold). There is no onfocus=this.blur() and no focusin re-grab: a keyboard user can Tab to every button, focus RESTS on it, and Space/Enter toggles aria-pressed. Boundary variant proving mouse-only focus suppression is not F55.
mechanism: mousedown -> preventDefault() cancels the default MOUSE focus assignment only (it fires on physical pointer press, never on Tab), so keyboard focus is never removed: focus lands on the toolbar button and remains, and the click handler toggles aria-pressed. F55's passing condition ('focus remains there until user moves it') holds for the keyboard path.

aspectTitle: Keystroke-timing dependence: functions that require specific timing of individual keystrokes (Test 4.B / second SC limb)
aspectDescription: The second normative limb of 2.1.1: 'without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes.' A function may be fully keyboard-reachable and activatable yet still FAIL because it demands a timing of keystrokes that keyboard-interface users (especially speech-input, sip-and-puff, switch, and on-screen-keyboard users) cannot reliably produce: keys that must be held down for an extended period before registering, multiple keystrokes that must be entered within a short window, double-press/rapid-repeat shortcuts with a tight interval, or input where the speed/rhythm of typing is itself part
scenario: SaaS account 'Danger zone': the 'Delete account' button is a real, focusable, named <button> wired for keyboard, but its keydown/keyup handler only fires the destructive action once Enter/Space has been HELD continuously for 2000 ms. A normal tap of Enter (keydown immediately followed by keyup) never reaches the threshold and does nothing; no other keyboard control deletes the account.
mechanism: Keystroke-HOLD-duration gate (2.1.1 second limb): activation requires a single key to be held for an extended period (2 s). Discrete-activation users (switch, sip-and-puff, speech input, on-screen keyboard, scanning) cannot emit a 2-second-long held keystroke, and no untimed keyboard path to the function exists, so Test 4.B has no passing path.

scenario: Public-transit trip planner with a route map. The 'center on your live location / turn on real-time vehicle tracking' function is bound to a documented G keyboard shortcut, but the handler fires geolocation only when two G keydown events arrive within 250 ms of each other. A single press of G arms a window but does nothing; two presses >250 ms apart never fire; there is no single-press button or menu item for the same function.
mechanism: Rapid double-press gate (2.1.1 second limb): the only trigger for an essential function (geolocation/live tracking) is two keystrokes within a 250 ms inter-keypress window. Speech-input (one key at a time), switch/scanning (slow cadence), tremor, and on-screen-keyboard users cannot produce a sub-250 ms double-press, and no single-press/untimed alternative exists.

scenario: Online-banking sign-in form (member number + 6-digit PIN). A hidden 'keystroke-dynamics' layer measures the interval between consecutive PIN keystrokes and rejects the login as an identity-verification failure if any gap exceeds 400 ms — even when the PIN entered is exactly correct. Visible help frames it as security ('we verify how you type'). No slow-typing-tolerant or alternative sign-in path is offered.
mechanism: Typing speed/rhythm as authentication (2.1.1 second limb; the exact Trusted Tester Test 4.B example). Successful sign-in requires each PIN keystroke gap to be fast (<=400 ms). Slow typists, on-screen-keyboard, switch/scanning, sip-and-puff, speech-input, and paste users supply the correct credential but fail the rhythm check; the timed login is the only mechanism, so no untimed keyboard path exists.

scenario: Payment confirmation screen ($248 rent). The primary control is a 'Hold to slide & pay' slider that confirms only after the Space bar is held for 1500 ms (a keystroke-timing barrier on its own), BUT directly beneath it the page provides a plain 'Confirm payment' button that completes the identical payment with a single, untimed Enter/Space press. Both paths invoke the same pay() function.
mechanism: Test 4.B allowance: a timed path (Space-hold slider, HOLD_MS=1500) coexists with an untimed keyboard method for the same function (single discrete activation of button#confirmBtn). Because a keyboard method free of specific keystroke timing is provided, the second limb of 2.1.1 is satisfied despite the slider's hold requirement.

scenario: Limited e-commerce drop (keycaps). The founders' discount code is revealed only when the visitor enters the Konami-style combo Up Up Down Down B A with each keystroke landing within 600 ms of the previous one; any slower gap resets the sequence to the start. The revealed code is the ONLY way to obtain the founders' price — no 'reveal code' button, link, or alternative exists.
mechanism: Multiple keystrokes within a short period of time (2.1.1 second limb): an essential commercial function (obtaining the discounted price) requires a six-key burst with sub-600 ms gaps. Switch/scanning, speech-input, sip-and-puff, on-screen-keyboard, and tremor users cannot complete the burst before it resets, and the timed sequence is the sole route to the code, so no untimed keyboard path exists.

scenario: Longform photo essay with a 4-photo gallery. The carousel is focusable and documents an arrow-key interaction, but a single press of the Right arrow never advances it: the handler is debounced to require three Right keydown events within 500 ms before moving one photo, and the burst counter resets if presses come too slowly. There is no single-press 'Next' button, slide-dots, or any other untimed advance control.
mechanism: Rapid repeated keystrokes required within a short period (2.1.1 second limb): advancing the gallery requires three Right presses inside a 500 ms window. A keyboard user pressing Right once, waiting, and pressing again (normal cadence for switch, scanning, speech-input, sip-and-puff, on-screen-keyboard, tremor users) never accumulates a burst and stays frozen on photo 1; no single-press/untimed control advances the carousel.
